extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, humorists, literary students, critics, and anyone studying theory of comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic framework for producing and recognizing comic effects in situations, character, and language; presents general methods (repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference) and how they project onto words and sentences. Useful for writers, dramatists, and critics who want concrete devices and examples to create or analyse humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition (comic reproduction of scenes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation (combination of circumstances) is repeated several times in its original form within a progressing series of events, creating a contrast with life's continual change and producing comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most laughable when the repeated scene is complex and naturally introduced (the playwright must reconcile complexity and likelihood). Classic examples: Moliere's Ecole des femmes and George Dandin repeat a single incident in three 'tempi'; contemporary light comedy may re-place the same series of incidents act after act or transpose them among different groups (masters vs servants). Use repetition to create a mathematical order of events that remains plausible to the audience. Beware of making repetition feel artificial—prepare the audience gradually so the coincidence becomes acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (roles/situations reversed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverse a situation or invert roles (subject ↔ object, superior ↔ subordinate) so that the expected order is turned upside-down; comedy arises when a character is trapped by his own scheme or when typical power relations are reversed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: prisoner lecturing magistrate, child teaching parents, robber robbed, the villain victim of his own villainy (the cheat cheated). In farce and comedy this often appears as a trap that recoils on the author of the plot. The device can be explicit onstage or only present in the audience's mind (we imagine the reversed situation). Useful for satirical refutation by swapping subject/object positions. Watch for overuse—straight inversion is the least subtle of the three major methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference of independent series (equivocal situations/misunderstanding)
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation belongs simultaneously to two independent series of events and can be interpreted in two entirely different meanings at once; the collision or coincidence of these series produces the comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes stage-made misunderstandings (each actor interprets only his series while the audience sees both), the equivocal situation, and transpositions between past and present series (e.g., Tartarin manacled to Bonivard). The author must continually remind the audience of the independence and coincidence (threaten dissolution of the partnership between series and then patch it up) to keep the comic tension. Useful in mock-heroic, in plays that embed a smaller comedy within a larger one, and when two temporal or social series intersect unexpectedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisation of life / absentmindedness as source of comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy seeks a 'mechanisation' of life—treating actions and relations as repeatable, reversible, and interchangeable; the ludicrous arises from absentmindedness, rigidity or automatic behaviour in persons or events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effects are produced when life is shown as jointed, machine-like (a dancing-doll) rather than a continuous irreversibly evolving organism. Both events and character laughability often result from lapses of attention or habitual formulas (ready-made phrases, stereotyped gestures). This explains why exaggerating natural absentmindedness into a system yields light comedy. Practical implication: exaggerate repetitive/rigid patterns to reveal an underlying mechanicality, but keep a thin link to plausible life so the effect remains acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: comic expressed vs comic created by language
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic expressed: humour that could be translated because it relies on situational/life-based elements. Comic created by language: humour that wholly depends on sentence structure, word choice, and the peculiarities of a language and therefore resists translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for language-based comedy, focus on the structure and idioms of the target language (puns, gender mismatches, stock phrase manipulations). For cross-cultural or translatable comedy, rely on situations, repetition, inversion, or reciprocal interference that don't depend on linguistic quirks. Example: many of M. Prudhomme's sayings are comic in French but lose effect when translated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit (esprit) as dramatic/diachronic thinking — wit as compressed comic scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit is a form of comic that consists of seeing ideas 'sub specie theatri'—making them converse like persons—and so producing quick, subtle comic scenes; witty remarks are the comic in a highly volatile state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A witty saying typically suggests a miniature scene; to analyse wit, expand the remark into a regular scene and classify it by the comic category it belongs to. Witty remarks often target interlocutors, absent persons, or society at large by twisting a current idea into a paradox or turning a phrase back on its author. Use wit for rapid comic effect, but recognise it is essentially a distilled form of the comic mechanisms applied to thought and language.

rubrics_metrics.name: General method for analysing or creating wit (enlarge remark into scene)
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand or craft witty remarks, enlarge the remark into a full scene and identify which comic method (repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference) the scene exemplifies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This chemical reduction shows that wit is not a separate species but the comic in miniature; when creating a witticism, imagine its full dramatic expansion to test its comic logic and root cause. Example: Mme. de Sévigné's 'Your chest hurts me' expands into a Moliere scene where diagnosing the child by the parent's pulse reveals the implied jointedness/sympathy between persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic transformation of sentences — three fundamental laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences become comic when one of three transformations is applied: repetition (transposition/repetition in a different key), inversion (reversing grammatical roles), or reciprocal interference (two independent sets of ideas coexist in one sentence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same three laws that govern events to series of words. Each law yields different kinds of verbal humour: inversion (subject/object swap) for refutation or irony, reciprocal interference for puns and true word-plays, and transposition for stylistic mismatch. Use these as a checklist when crafting verbal humour; predict how the audience will supply the 'natural' variant and enjoy the mismatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion applied to sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverse syntactic or semantic roles in a sentence (put subject in place of object etc.) to obtain a comic meaning or to refute an idea humorously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common among professional wits who test whether reversing a sentence yields a joke (e.g., 'What do you mean by emptying your pipe on to my terrace?' — 'What do you mean by putting your terrace under my pipe?'). Effective for retorts and repartee; less rich than other sentence-transformations so use sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference in sentences (pun vs play on words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a sentence that simultaneously expresses (or appears to express) two independent meanings; ranges from homophonic puns to sophisticated single-sentence plays where a word's literal/figurative senses clash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puns are the most superficial/reprobate form (different words/sounds masquerading as one). A truer word-play uses the same sentence with legitimately different meanings (literal vs figurative). The comic results from a momentary lapse of language's usual function; the audience detects the double sense. Use for quick, surprising effects, but be aware of tastes—puns can be cheap unless elevated by context or cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition (stylistic/key mismatch of language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfer ideas into an inappropriate style or key—expressing a naturally-styled idea in a very different register so that the audience automatically supplies the original and feels the comic displacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transposition in language is analogous to repetition in action: putting the same idea in an unexpected stylistic environment (e.g., lofty phrasing about trivial things) produces comedy. Because the audience knows the 'natural' phrasing, presenting only the transposed one is often enough. This is fertile for satirical and mock-heroic effects. Example: Labiche's use of mismatched diction and the insertion of a 'smaller comedy' inside a larger one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity inserted into ready-made phrase-forms (automatism revealed)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic meaning is obtained when an absurd idea is fitted into a well-established, ready-made phrase-form so the automatism of speech is revealed and the absurdity surfaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: M. Prudhomme saying 'Ce sabre est le plus beau jour de ma vie'—the absurdity inside a stock phrase exposes automatic utterance. Combining two hackneyed sayings so the ear treats them as one (dovetailing clichés) also produces this effect. Use known idioms and slip an absurd or incompatible ending to make the automatism visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materialising metaphors / taking figurative expressions literally
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic effect is achieved whenever we deliberately treat a figurative expression as literal, drawing attention to a word's physical/concrete sense rather than its moral/figurative meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many words have both physical and moral meanings, literalising metaphors produces visible, often ludicrous, concrete images (e.g., 'Tous les arts sont soeurs' vs 'soeurs' gender mismatch; 'He is always running after a joke' → 'He won't catch it'). Use concrete imagery borrowed from a different semantic field (sport, physical action) to materialise an abstract phrase and provoke laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language rigidity / inelasticity and momentum as comic causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Speaking or doing something one had no intention of—because of momentum, automatism, or rigid phraseology—can be comic when the utterance evidences a lack of active attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and exploit stereotyped formulas or speech habits that reveal the speaker's automatic mode. A phrase that, when separated from the speaker, still betrays automatic utterance (because it contains absurdity or contradiction), will be comic. Craft characters with habitual linguistic tics to generate predictable-but-amusing lapses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanding symbols/emblems on their concrete side
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a symbol or emblem (medal, phrase, metaphor) and expand it literally so that its concrete implications are exploited for comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a Monte Carlo official says he 'staked his medal on a number' and treats the medal as a literal gambling stake; a bride 'entitled to oranges' or wearing orange-blossoms. This literal extension of emblematic language creates a visual/comic incongruity. Use when you want a punchline that hinges on treating a figurative object as if materially exchangeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining commonplace phrase-forms (dovetailing hackneyed sayings) to deceive the ear
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose a sentence by joining two or more familiar sentences/phrases so they sound like a single accepted formula until the combined meaning reveals an absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This plays on the audience's expectation and momentary inattention; examples include combining 'It is God who disposes of the lives of men' with 'It is criminal for a man to kill his fellow-creature' to produce a surprising, laughable collision. Use subtle linkage of clichés to lull attention and then subvert it with an absurd synthesis.
